summary: Describes an approach for providing RSVP resource reservation services across IP tunnels. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: Reserving a fast lane works on normal roads. This explains how to also reserve it inside a hidden tunnel.

subtitle: How tunnel endpoints run RSVP between themselves so end-to-end reservations can cross an IP-in-IP tunnel.

tldr.problem: RSVP messages and data inside an IP-in-IP tunnel are wrapped in an outer header that intermediate routers cannot tell apart, so reservations cannot cover the tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: The tunnel entry and exit routers run a second, recursive RSVP session between themselves. Data that has a reservation is wrapped in an outer IP and UDP header, and a new SESSION_ASSOC object ties each end-to-end session to its tunnel session.
tldr.outcome: End-to-end reservations can be carried over a tunnel with changes only at its two ends. If an endpoint does not support the scheme, the tunnel acts as a best-effort link.

today: RFC 2746 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the RSVP specification in RFC 2205.

sections.title: The Problem with Tunnels
sections.content:
IP-in-IP tunnels are widely used to carry datagrams through parts of the network that do not directly support a service, or to change routing behaviour, for example for multicast, mobile IP or virtual private networks. To deploy the RSVP framework (RFC 2205) flexibly, it is desirable for tunnels to act as RSVP-controllable links.

Today that does not work. RSVP packets entering a tunnel get an outer IP header with a protocol number other than 46 (for IP-in-IP it is 4) and no Router-Alert option, which makes them invisible to RSVP routers between the tunnel endpoints. And with only an IP header as wrapper, nothing distinguishes packets that use reservations from those that do not, or packets of different RSVP sessions.

This document describes an enhancement that lets RSVP make reservations across IP-in-IP tunnels, with minimal changes to RSVP and the integrated services framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a message goes into a tunnel, the roads inside cannot see who is in the car, so they cannot give anyone a reserved lane.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Tunnel
sections.content:
A tunnel, like any link, can take part in an RSVP-aware network in one of three ways.

  • Type 1: no reservation or QoS support at all; a best-effort link. This is also what you get when an endpoint does not support this scheme.
  • Type 2: the link can promise some overall level of resources but not allocate it to individual flows, such as a statically configured allocation.
  • Type 3: the link can reserve for individual end-to-end flows, with tunnel reservations created and torn down dynamically as end-to-end reservations come and go.

A tunnel may also mix type 2 and type 3 behaviour, and how an end-to-end session is treated is a matter of local policy. A tunnel whose reservation cannot be adjusted is a hard pipe; one whose reserved amount can be adjusted is a soft pipe.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tunnels have no reserved lane, some have one shared lane, and some can open a private lane for each traveller.

sections.title: Recursive RSVP and Session Binding
sections.content:
The design goals are to coexist with most current IP-in-IP schemes, change RSVP as little as possible, touch only the two tunnel endpoints, and interoperate with routers that have not been upgraded, in which case the tunnel behaves as a non-RSVP link.

The basic idea is to apply RSVP recursively over the tunnel. The entry router Rentry sends PATH messages and the exit router Rexit sends RESV messages for tunnel sessions, using one or more Fixed-Filter style unicast reservations. The end-to-end session sees the tunnel as one logical link.

Packets that need a reservation are wrapped with an IP and a UDP header, and the UDP port numbers distinguish different sessions. All sessions between the same two routers share source address, destination address and destination UDP port; the source port identifies the session.

To tell Rexit which tunnel session an end-to-end session maps to, the RFC weighs three options (a new message, a new object on end-to-end PATH messages, or UDP-encapsulating the PATH messages) and chooses the new object because it is simpler and works even if Rexit does not support the scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends of the tunnel act like a sender and receiver, and hand each traveller a ticket number so both ends know which reserved lane belongs to whom.

sections.title: The SESSION_ASSOC and NODE_CHAR Objects
sections.content:
The SESSION_ASSOC object, class 192, carries the end-to-end SESSION object and the Sender FILTER-SPEC of the tunnel session it maps to. Ctype is sent as zero and ignored on receipt. Rentry adds it to end-to-end PATH messages, and Rexit records the association and removes the object before forwarding.

The NODE_CHAR object lets Rexit tell Rentry that it supports this scheme, through a single T bit. Its length is eight and the proposed class is 128, in the range that unknown receivers drop without an error report. Rexit appends it to RESV messages sent to Rentry, and Rentry removes it before forwarding upstream. A Rentry that does not support the scheme simply ignores it.
sections.plainLanguage: One note says which tunnel lane a traveller uses. Another note, with a single tick box, says that the far end knows how to do all this.

sections.title: Handling RSVP Messages at the Endpoints
sections.content:
Rentry encapsulates end-to-end PATH messages and sends them to Rexit. When the matching RESV reaches Rexit with a NODE_CHAR object attached, Rentry decides, from the PATH and RESV contents and local policy, whether and how to map the session. It then either creates a new tunnel session or adds to an existing one, and sends a PATH with SESSION_ASSOC. Rexit answers the tunnel PATH with a tunnel RESV that reserves resources inside the tunnel.

If an end-to-end PATH arrives at Rexit without SESSION_ASSOC, Rexit sets the Non_RSVP flag and the global break bit in the ADSPEC, unless it can safely use the tunnel sessions' worst-case parameters. With SESSION_ASSOC, Rexit composes the tunnel session's ADSPEC parameters into the end-to-end ADSPEC.

For a hard pipe, a request that would exceed the tunnel reservation is an admission control failure and a RESV_ERR with error code 01 goes back. For a soft pipe the tunnel reservation can be adjusted when end-to-end reservations arrive, change or leave, and the RFC suggests some hysteresis. A configured tunnel session stays active even when its last end-to-end session goes away. One stated limitation: the first RESV of an end-to-end session fixes its mapping for as long as the reservation is active.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry gate and exit gate exchange notes, agree on a lane, and the exit gate reserves it. If a lane is too small, the request is refused.

sections.title: Forwarding Data and Other Details
sections.content:
Rentry uses the IP+UDP encapsulation only when a resource reservation, not just PATH state, is actually in place for the tunnel session that matches the packet. Otherwise it uses the tunnel's normal format. That keeps data decodable at Rexit.

The source UDP port is chosen by Rentry when it sets up the tunnel session, and conveyed in SESSION_ASSOC. The destination port should be the one assigned by IANA, 363. Errors on a tunnel session are relayed by Rentry or Rexit back to the end host. Since UDP-encapsulated packets should not be fragmented, entry routers must support tunnel MTU discovery as in RFC 2003, or can use the Path MTU Discovery mechanism of RFC 2210.

When several end-to-end sessions share one tunnel session, an aggregate Tspec is needed. The RFC leaves the semantics open; the simplest way is a sum, as in the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed service specifications (RFC 2211, RFC 2212).
sections.plainLanguage: Only travellers who really hold a reserved lane get the special wrapper. Everyone else goes through the tunnel the normal way.

sections.title: IPsec, Multicast Tunnels and Security
sections.content:
When the tunnel uses IPsec, especially ESP in tunnel mode, the tunnel session uses the GPI SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE/FILTER_SPEC from RFC 2207. Data packets then get no UDP header because the SPI can classify them, and user oriented keying must give reserved and best-effort packets different SPIs.

The RFC also sketches multicast tunnels and multipoint tunnels, noting that concrete details are left for future versions. For multipoint tunnels endpoints MUST NOT make wildcard reservations.

On security, the scheme adds no new issues beyond those of RSVP and tunnels. The major RSVP issue is controlling and authenticating access to enhanced quality of service, and message integrity is protected as described in RFC 2747.
sections.plainLanguage: If the tunnel is already locked with a secret code, the code number is used to spot reserved traffic. It is only as safe as the tunnel and RSVP themselves.
